questions.q: What is dense (vector) search prone to missing?
options: Exact terms like a specific product code or rare acronym, if nothing nearby reads as semantically close
Any result at all, regardless of the query
Results written in a language other than English
Anything stored with metadata attached
questions.explain: An embedding model smooths meaning together, which is its strength for paraphrase but can cause it to under-rank a chunk that only matches on an exact, specific term.

questions.q: What does sparse (keyword) search, like BM25, do well that dense search doesn't?
options: It eliminates the need for a vector database entirely
It reliably matches exact or near-exact terms, like a specific product code
It automatically translates queries into other languages
It stores vectors with fewer dimensions
questions.explain: Sparse/keyword search is built around exact term matching, which is exactly what dense embedding search can sometimes under-rank.

questions.q: In the fusion diagram from Qdrant's documentation shown in this lesson, what does the "Fusion" step do?
options: It deletes all results that don't appear in both lists
It converts sparse vectors into dense vectors
It merges the independently ranked dense results list and sparse results list into one combined ranked list
It re-embeds every document using a new model
questions.explain: The diagram shows two separate rankings — dense and sparse — both feeding into a fusion step that produces one combined "mixture" list drawing from both.

questions.q: In Reciprocal Rank Fusion (RRF), what does a document's score depend on?
options: The raw cosine similarity score only
Its rank (1st, 2nd, 3rd...) in each result list, scored as 1 / (k + rank) and summed across lists
Only whether it appears in the sparse list at all
The number of words in the document
questions.explain: RRF avoids comparing scores on different scales (cosine similarity vs. a keyword score) by working with each document's rank position in each list instead, summing 1 / (k + rank) across every list it appears in.

questions.q: In the worked RRF example in this lesson (k = 60), why does doc_B (dense rank 3, keyword rank 1) outscore doc_A (dense rank 1, keyword rank 4)?
options: Because doc_A was excluded from the sparse list entirely
Because doc_B appeared earlier alphabetically
Because RRF always favors the second document listed
Because doc_B ranked well in both lists, and RRF rewards consistently good ranking across multiple lists over being the single best result in only one
questions.explain: Computing the formula gives doc_B a combined score of about 0.0323 versus doc_A's about 0.0320 — RRF's summing behavior means strong-in-both beats best-in-one-only.
